note.headline: Meta slips 1.3% to 589.82 below resistance; wait for 2027-01-27 earnings

summary.thesis: Meta's sales are still growing fast, but margins and free cash flow have fallen sharply, and the price already assumes a strong cash-flow recovery that the reports have not yet shown.
summary.decision: Long-term: wait. Swing: no trade while the price stays under resistance in a downtrend.
summary.act_at: Buy near 475.85; swing only after a close above 615.4

note.happening: Meta closed at 589.82, down 1.3% on the day. That puts it back below the 591.53–605.33 resistance zone, which has turned the price back 7 times, and just above the 576.61–586.24 support zone. CNBC reported that Meta is using Instagram to get an ad boost from its Muse personal AI agent. The next earnings report is due 2027-01-27.
note.business: Demand still looks healthy. Revenue over the last twelve months was 241.6B, up from 189.5B, a growth rate of 27.53%. But growth is slowing: quarterly growth was 26.07% versus 33.08% two quarters earlier. The bigger change is in profits and cash. The operating margin (the share of sales left after running costs) fell to 32.86% from 43.23%, and free cash flow (the cash left after spending on the business) fell to 28.6B from 44.8B. With R&D at 31.68% of revenue, heavy spending is the likely cause (general knowledge: this is mostly the AI build-out). The balance sheet has moved from a cash cushion to roughly even: cash is 11.2B, debt is 83.7B, and net cash is -1.2B. Available liquidity of 82.4B means there is no funding risk. The filings flag a 29% miss against forecasts last quarter and earnings per share lagging behind sales. The Muse report is a product story. It could help ad demand later, but for now it affects sentiment, not reported numbers. Insider sales of $14.1M outside pre-set plans are a governance note and do not change the business. What is at risk: margins and cash flow. What is not at risk: the scale of demand and the 81.03% gross margin.

worth.text: The methods disagree because they ask different questions. A discounted cash flow (DCF) values the business on the cash it produces today, which is 28.6B. On that basis, fair value is 240.52 in the bear case, 372.24 in the base case and 506.03 in the bull case, so the price sits above every DCF value. To justify 589.82, free cash flow would need to start growing at about 35.8% a year. Even 30% starting growth gives only 476.95. Meta's own price-to-sales history, which ignores the cash drop, puts value between 475.85 and 707.21 (low to mid), and 881.21 at the high end. On simple multiples the stock does not look stretched: 20.2 times trailing earnings and 6.3 times sales, against a peer median of 6.1. Its price-to-sales also sits at the 33rd percentile of its own five-year range. The gap between methods comes down to one thing: whether free cash flow returns to its earlier level or stays where it is now. If the operating margin fell to 24%, the value would drop to 244.63.
worth.key_assumption: Free cash flow recovers toward the earlier 44.8B as the heavy spending pays off, instead of staying near 28.6B.
